procedural_history.impugned_order: Order made on the 13th October 1955 in Civil Application No. 1506 of 1955, suspending the respondent from practice as an Advocate for a period of one year.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court received a report from the Bar Council Tribunal. The Tribunal held the allegations in Mr. Sonavane's report to be proved based on the respondent's admission and recommended serious notice be taken of the respondent's conduct. The High Court, after considering the report, found the respondent's misconduct serious and imposed a one-year suspension from practice.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The respondent's application for a certificate of fitness for appeal to the Supreme Court was refused by the High Court. The respondent then filed a petition for special leave to appeal before the Supreme Court, which was dismissed. The Supreme Court then issued a rule for disciplinary action against the Advocate based on the report from the Bombay High Court. The Supreme Court is now dealing with the rule for disciplinary action, considering the respondent's response and arguments.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should hold a fresh inquiry into the advocate's misconduct.

facts: The advocate had previously admitted to the truth of the magistrate's report (the Sonavane report) regarding his misconduct before the High Court and the Bar Council Tribunal.
He had confessed his guilt and tendered an unconditional apology, hoping for a lenient outcome.
When the High Court suspended him for one year, he changed his position before the Supreme Court.

In his petition to the Supreme Court, he made only vague allegations that the report was an "exaggerated, garbled and manifestly incorrect version" of events, without pointing to any specific inaccuracies.
application: The Supreme Court viewed the advocate's request for a new inquiry as a change in tactics.
The Court reasoned that the advocate had initially admitted guilt to avoid a full inquiry, likely hoping his apology would be sufficient.
When this strategy failed and he received a suspension from the High Court, he then tried to retract his admission and demand an inquiry.
The Court found it unacceptable for the advocate to "go back on" his previous unconditional admission based on such vague new allegations.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the request for a fresh inquiry, stating that it would not permit the advocate to "play with the Court" by changing his tactics after his initial strategy of admitting guilt and apologizing failed to secure the lenient outcome he desired.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should consider the legality of the proceedings before the Bombay High Court or the Bar Council Tribunal.

facts: The respondent (the advocate) had previously filed a petition for special leave to appeal the judgment and order of the Bombay High Court.
The Supreme Court had already dismissed that petition for appeal.
law: The Supreme Court cited its own previous observation in the case of 'In the matter of Mr. G, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court'.
application: The Court pointed out to the respondent that since his application to appeal the High Court's decision had been dismissed, the Supreme Court was not concerned with the legality of the proceedings in the Bombay High Court or before the Bar Council Tribunal in the context of the current disciplinary rule.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided not to consider the legality of the earlier proceedings because the advocate's direct appeal on that matter had already been dismissed. Therefore, the issue could not be re-examined in the separate disciplinary action initiated by the Supreme Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should hold a fresh inquiry into the advocate's misconduct.
appellant_arguments: The respondent had already admitted the truth of the report before the High Court and cannot be permitted to go back on his admission based on vague allegations.
The respondent's request for a new inquiry is merely a change in tactics after his initial strategy of confessing and apologizing failed to prevent his suspension by the High Court.
respondent_arguments: The report on his conduct was an "exaggerated, garbled and manifestly incorrect version" of the events.
He was "more or less compelled to tender a humiliating apology."
A proper inquiry should be held by or under the directions of the Supreme Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should consider the legality of the proceedings before the Bombay High Court or the Bar Council Tribunal.
appellant_arguments: The Supreme Court, in this disciplinary Rule, is not concerned with the prior proceedings because the respondent's application for special leave to appeal from the High Court's judgment had already been dismissed.
respondent_arguments: The Tribunal had no jurisdiction because the alleged misconduct was not committed in his capacity as an Advocate, but as an accused person appearing in person.
The Tribunal acted with prejudice and bias, failed to formulate a formal charge, and unfairly reversed an earlier decision on its own jurisdiction without giving him a hearing.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Court will not permit a party to retract a prior unconditional admission of facts on the basis of vague, unsubstantiated allegations.
obiter: It is needless for us to emphasise that a person holding the responsible position of an Advocate of a High Court should be even more careful about the statements he makes.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the advocate's conduct during a criminal trial where he was the accused, though not committed in his professional capacity, constituted "other misconduct" under the Bar Councils Act. His behavior was a persistent attempt to be rude to the Magistrate and bring the administration of justice into contempt, which is unworthy of a member of the legal profession. The Court refused his request for a new inquiry, viewing it as an impermissible change in tactics after he had already admitted his guilt before the High Court in the hope of receiving a lighter penalty.
legal_tests_applied: the Indian Legislature by using the words "professional or other misconduct" in section 10 of the Indian Bar Councils Act intended to confer on the Court disciplinary jurisdiction to take action in all cases of misconduct whether in a professional or other capacity .leaving it to the discretion of Court to take action only in suitable cases.
why_respondent_won: The advocate admitted the correctness of the report on his misconduct, confessed his guilt, and tendered an unconditional apology before the High Court, and cannot be permitted to change tactics and ask for a new inquiry after that strategy failed.

The advocate's conduct, which included being persistently rude to and contemptuous of the Magistrate and attempting to hold up the trial, was indefensible and brought the administration of justice into contempt, meriting severe condemnation and suspension.
The Court has jurisdiction to take disciplinary action for "other misconduct" committed in a non-professional capacity, as the Bar Councils Act is not limited to only professional misconduct.
policy_considerations: An Advocate... cannot be permitted to play with the Court in the way this Advocate has done. He admitted the correctness of the report, confessed his guilt and tendered an unconditional apology evidently in the hope that he would get away with it by merely tendering an apology. Finding that the tactics did not work with the High Court as he expected the same to do, he now wants to change his tactics by asking for an enquiry which he had himself avoided by means of his admission and apology. This we are not prepared to permit him to do.
Any suspension for a period less than the period fixed by the Bombay High Court will obviously lead to serious anomaly and inconvenience.
